name: Trace line art to vectors
description: turn a raster picture of line art into real vector paths — open centrelines for strokes with a recovered per-path width, closed contours for regions too solid to have a centreline, and one colour per pen it finds
phrases: vectorise a PNG of line art
turn a raster drawing into editable paths
get centrelines out of a scanned drawing
convert a generated image of line art into real vector art
split a coloured drawing into one layer per pen
trace a drawing into a scene
get named elements out of a raster drawing

requires.note: the pipeline itself — binarize, split fills, thin, graph, fit
numpy and opencv-python; without them the entry fails with an ImportError

returns: the SVG on stdout -- a bare <g> by default, a standalone document with --svg -- or to the file named by -o. With --scene it emits a scene document instead (named elements, a frame carrying the page transform, and the source's digest as provenance), which is what every `scene.*` capability takes. A one-line report of size, stroke and fill counts, curve count and the pens found goes to stderr
notes: --scene IS THE ONE THAT COMPOSES. The SVG output is flat and unnamed and nothing in this toolkit reads it back; `--scene` emits a `scene.document`, which every `scene.*` capability accepts. This record does not declare `produces` because the default output is SVG and a record may name one schema, not one per flag. SVG goes to STDOUT and the report to STDERR, so piping the output into a file is safe but reading the report from stdout gets nothing. An unreadable source exits 2 with `lineart-trace: cannot read <path>` — but OpenCV prints its own `[ WARN:0@<elapsed>]` line before it, and the elapsed time in that line changes every run, so this is recorded here rather than as an example: an example that cannot reproduce is worse than none. SVG goes to STDOUT and the report to STDERR, so piping the output into a file is safe but reading the report from stdout gets nothing. Quality is not uniform across subjects and the limitations are measured rather than guessed: stipple and grey washes have no centreline to recover and come back as filled regions or nothing; lettering loses small counters; a flat fill covering more of the page than the paper does is read as the paper and the drawing comes out inside out. Judge fine line art by coverage and spill rather than IoU — a half-pixel offset costs a fixed absolute overlap, which is a large fraction of a 3px stroke and a small one of a 20px stroke. README.md has the full table.
